No going back: how the Iran war broke the old world order 

“The global order has been altered, and economies are unlikely to simply pick up where they left off before the U.S. and Israel began bombing Iran. The framework deal between the United States and Iran sets the stage for an end to the bursts of violence and debilitating disruption of energy deliveries and trade in the Persian Gulf. But don’t expect economies around the globe to simply pick up where they left off before the bombing began. The war has set in motion changes that will be hard to reverse,” 
writes The New York Times.

Because of the crisis in the Persian Gulf, the United States lost its status as a 'guarantor of stability,' as Iranian strikes hit American allies despite U.S. defenses, eroding trust and pushing Gulf states like Saudi Arabia to seek direct deals with Iran. Meanwhile, European and Asian nations are accelerating their shift to renewables — not just for climate goals, but to reduce reliance on a volatile region under U.S. influence, whose stability can no longer be assumed. Though the U.S. has temporarily filled some energy gaps for allies like Japan and South Korea, the war has permanently reinforced the strategic push toward energy independence from the Persian Gulf.

🔻 Iran, Pakistan vow to strengthen strategic ties

📌 Tehran, IRNA – President Masoud Pezeshkian and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif have emphasized the need for ongoing cooperation to strengthen peace and security, as well as to enhance the strategic relations between Tehran and Islamabad.

During a phone call on Thursday, Pezeshkian and Sharif discussed the latest developments regarding the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) and the processes moving forward between Iran and the United States. They exchanged views on the current state of bilateral relations and ways to enhance joint cooperation across various fields.
​
Pezeshkian expressed sincere gratitude for the compassionate, responsible, and diligent efforts of the Pakistani government in reducing tensions and advancing diplomatic initiatives.
​
He specifically thanked Prime Minister Sharif, Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Interior Minister Seyyed Mohsin Naqvi for their roles and constructive cooperation in the mediation process that led to the initial agreement to end the war between Iran and the United States.
​
Emphasizing that such an approach—rooted in good faith, Islamic brotherhood, and regional responsibility from Pakistani officials—was a valuable manifestation of empathy and collaboration between the two nations, Pezeshkian said, “The sincere and diligent efforts of the government and people of Pakistan during this critical juncture will remain in the historical memory of the Iranian nation. The Islamic Republic of Iran will always be grateful for this benevolent solidarity.”
​
He also expressed hope that the agreement reached would pave the way for lasting peace, reduced tensions, and the initiation of a new phase of regional cooperation in the interest of the nations in the region.
​
For his part, Sharif expressed his satisfaction with the recent agreement signed by the officials of the Islamic Republic of Iran, the United States, and Pakistan, describing the deal as an important step toward enhancing regional stability and security.
​
He also noted that Iran and Pakistan are more than just neighboring countries; they are friendly and brotherly nations with deep historical, cultural, and religious ties.
​
Referring to the vast capacities for cooperation between Tehran and Islamabad, Sharif emphasized his country’s interest in developing and deepening bilateral relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran in the fields of science and technology, industry, agriculture, trade, economy, and other areas of mutual interest.
​
The two sides emphasized the ongoing consultations, the enhancement of bilateral cooperation, and the use of all available resources to improve the strategic relations between the two countries.

Ray Kurzweil, the futurist who predicted the internet, smartphones, and AI says aging ends by 2032 (Save this)

Kurzweil, now 78 years old, told a live audience that humanity will reach longevity escape velocity by 2032 and he explained exactly what that means with mathematical precision.

Right now, for every year you live, you get back approximately five months of life expectancy from medical and scientific progress meaning you are losing roughly seven months of net life per calendar year.

Longevity escape velocity is the threshold where that ratio flips, for every year you live, you get back a full year or more from scientific progress, meaning your biological clock starts running backward.

Kurzweil's prediction is that threshold hits by 2032 and beyond that point, you do not simply stop dying of aging, you actively get younger every year.

The mechanism is AI-driven drug discovery at a scale that was physically impossible five years ago.

By 2030, Kurzweil argues, AI will be able to take a biological problem, generate millions of potential drug candidates, screen all of them, and run trials on simulated digital populations compressing decades of clinical research into weeks.

This is already happening.

David Sinclair's lab at Harvard used AI to virtually screen 8 billion molecules against aging targets and is now preparing human trials moving from $400,000 gene therapies toward a $100 pill that can reset biological age by 50 to 95% in four weeks.

Sinclair has already demonstrated the ability to reverse aging in mammals restoring sight in mice with optic nerve damage and reversing Alzheimer's symptoms in lab models.

Kurzweil's track record is what makes the 2032 claim impossible to dismiss.

He predicted the internet's global dominance in 1990, the defeat of a world chess champion by a computer in 1998, pocket-sized devices as primary communications tools in 1999, and AI passing professional exams in the mid-2020s, all before anyone else was saying it publicly.

If you are under 60 and in reasonable health, his message is stay alive, stay healthy, and get to 2032.

The tools on the other side of that date will be unlike anything medicine has ever produced.

Uranium In, Dollars Out

The leaked MoU makes the trade‑off brutally clear: this is not disarmament, it is a risk‑management swap dressed up as peace.

Iran’s enriched uranium stays inside the country, to be “diluted” under IAEA supervision rather than removed or destroyed. The infrastructure, the know‑how and the material base all remain onshore, convertible back into leverage if the politics or supervision change. 

At the same time, the memorandum says that, upon signing, the US and Iran will agree on a mechanism to make frozen funds and assets available, alongside Treasury waivers for crude, petroleum products and derivatives, and a US‑branded 300‑billion‑dollar reconstruction plan.

The middle articles speak the language of sovereignty and territorial integrity, plus a 60‑day “extendable” window to reach a final deal. 

The last ones speak the language of cash: sanctions relief, asset release, oil waivers, reconstruction money, and a promise to wrap the final package in a binding UN Security Council resolution. 

It is a structure designed to reassure markets and chancelleries first, then sort out the nuclear core later.

Look at the sequencing. The MoU does not demand deep nuclear steps before money starts moving; it locks in limits on US forces in the region, ends “military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” lifts the Hormuz blockade, and only then pushes the real nuclear bargaining into a 60‑day negotiating fog. 

The Strait of Hormuz clause is a lawyer’s dream: Iran commits to “use its best efforts” to ensure safe, toll‑free passage. If ever there was an invitation to creative obstruction once the immediate crisis passes, that’s it.

Politically, the architecture is almost elegant in its cynicism. Washington gets a ceasefire, cheaper oil and a talking point for the G7. 

Tehran keeps its program at home, diluted but not dismantled, secures sanctions easing and access to long‑frozen assets, and sees its leverage over regional security and shipping effectively baked into the system.

 Both capitals can claim victory. Neither has actually eliminated the underlying threat.

So yes, it is a memorandum that ends a war and restarts trade. By any honest standard, it is not the removal of the danger it was sold against; it is the formalization of a world in which enriched uranium stays in Iran, and the rest of us pay for the privilege of pretending that dilution is the same thing as disarmament.
